totally compromised

No. The attack from january 2014 to july 2014 only affected access to hidden services, which is the minority of activity on Tor. If you were using it as proxy, you were not affected. From the developers:

Unfortunately, it's still unclear what "affected" includes. We know the attack looked for users who fetched hidden service descriptors, but the attackers likely were not able to see any application-level traffic (e.g. what pages were loaded or even whether users visited the hidden service they looked up)

Further, the attack might have revealed locations of hidden services, but that only means the IP-address of the servers running the hidden service. While this is pretty bad for the anonymity, it is not equal to a break-in of the server where user data might be affected.

The attack probably also tried to learn who published hidden service descriptors, which would allow the attackers to learn the location of that hidden service.

So unless you were hosting a hidden service or tried to visit one in that time frame using one of the malicious entry nodes, this attack is of no concern to you.

but it's been cracked and there are now veritably effective attack methods for getting back in

No. The vulnerability has been closed in 0.2.4.23 (end of july 2014).

I'm no expert, but I believe it's biggest vulnerability is with exit nodes.

This particular attack had nothing to do with exit nodes. Generally speaking the exit nodes are the weakest point, but that is the case with every onion routing, including HORNET. So attacks usually are targeting exit nodes, but as far as I know, until today there has not been an attack that could positively de-anonymize large quantities of Tor users, who were using it as a proxy (which is the majority of cases).

There is one class of attacks that is looming over every onion routing protocol: Correlation attacks. This kind of attack requires monitoring a very large portion of all nodes in the network over a long period of time. Unfortunately there is very little research on this topic that would allow making accurate assessments and improve security. However, the most dangerous attacker would be one that can monitor the entire internet around Tor. From the information free'd by Snowden, we now know that at least until 2013 the NSA, being the only known entity with that much surveillance power, could not reliably do correlation attacks on Tor users. And they are surveilling and recording every Tor connection on the net indefinetely. So if they can't do it, you might assume that Tor is pretty damn secure.

Please don't buy into all that panic news that regularly demonstrates the journalists general lack of understanding. Spreading such news has a chilling effect and might prevent users who really need the anonymity from using one of the most promising solutions.

However as an in country anti-government or criminal communications network it doesn't do well. Because your accessing things within the same country one government would be able to monitor the traffic. This was a know flaw so they created "dark servers" servers that can only be access within the tor network, that way if you monitor all the traffic you still couldn't see it. The problem with this, like we saw with the first silk road, if the server operator is the government* then tor can't hide you.

Every other Saturday, the group (consisting of a maximum 12 children and 5 carers) meet at the local youth club. It's a small center with a kitchen, arts and crafts room, DJ booth and a large area with a ping pong table and two pool tables. The children we have, have disabilities such as autism, Asperger's Syndrome, Tourette's and some that just make loud sounds etc.. Well, the kids come and chill out for a bit, do what they want. And then, at around 11 - just before lunch - we go to the local supermarket, only five minutes away. We go there so that the kids can learn what it's like to be individual for their future lives.

So, what happened was, we were just going to the store and something absolutely disgusting happened. Also, let me say, these children do understand their situation, to an extent. Some of them understand that they're different to other children - they're not totally naive to their disabilities.
